title: Gumiho: Korea’s Nine-Tailed Fox, Fox Beads and Changing Stories
metaDescription: Gumiho is Korea’s nine-tailed fox figure. Tales include transformation, fox beads and unusual ancestry; they do not all follow one rule for becoming human.
description: Gumiho is Korea’s nine-tailed fox figure. Tales include transformation, fox beads and unusual ancestry; they do not all follow one rule for becoming human.
storyHooks: A child discovers that their family’s celebrated ancestor was a fox. Protecting the family reputation would mean erasing the person who saved it.

sections.origin: Gumiho literally refers to a nine-tailed fox. A Korea Heritage Agency essay also explains that Korean fox-spirit stories use the category more broadly than a strict tail count.
sections.legend: The essay discusses fox-bead stories: a pupil acquires extraordinary knowledge after swallowing a fox’s bead. It also presents a fox-woman ancestry tale about the general Gang Gam-chan. These give the fox roles beyond a single predatory stereotype.
sections.variants: Other stories are threatening, including the fox sister. A fixed requirement to eat a particular number of organs should not be treated as the rule of every gumiho tale. Identify the particular account before combining its details.
sections.culture: For writers, choose the relationship first: stranger, family member, teacher, or parent. Then decide which recorded motif your adaptation uses, and label the new choices as fiction.

sources.title: Korea Heritage Agency — Lee Young-soo, creatures in Korean folktales (2022)

researchNote: This introduction summarizes a named heritage essay. It does not claim to represent every regional fox tale.

questions.question: Are all gumiho evil?
questions.answer: The cited essay includes both harmful foxes and foxes connected with exceptional human ancestry or knowledge.

questions.question: Is a gumiho identical to a kitsune?
questions.answer: These names belong to different storytelling contexts. Comparing particular stories is more useful than treating the labels as interchangeable.
